summary: Describes the routing requirements placed on the GMPLS protocol suite so that it can support the capabilities of an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) as defined by the ITU-T. It covers time-division connections such as SONET and SDH and optical transport networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A smart optical network needs its map-sharing system to meet certain rules. This memo lists what those rules are for the GMPLS map system.

questions: what is a routing area in ason
what does gmpls routing need for ason
subtitle: What the ITU-T's optical control plane needs from GMPLS routing: nested routing areas, controllers and a common set of advertised attributes.

tldr.problem: The ITU-T defined an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) control plane, and the IETF needed to know what that asks of routing in the GMPLS protocol suite.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes ASON's routing architecture in its own terms: a network split into hierarchical Routing Areas, run by protocol-independent Routing Controllers, advertising a common set of node and link attributes.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. It deliberately proposes no protocol, extension or applicability analysis.

today: RFC 4258 is an Informational document from November 2005. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, and it sets out requirements rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Why ASON Needs Routing Requirements
sections.content:
The GMPLS protocol suite can control different switching technologies, including time-division (TDM) connections over SONET/SDH and Optical Transport Networks (OTNs). The ITU-T's control plane architecture for an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON), defined in G.8080, needs some further capabilities. This RFC captures the resulting routing requirements for GMPLS.

The ITU-T documents it summarizes (G.7715 and G.7715.1) are protocol-neutral. The RFC restates them in ASON terminology. It says plainly that GMPLS applicability, protocol design and suggested extensions are strictly outside its scope.

Five assumptions frame everything: the operator decides how to subdivide the network into Routing Areas; the routing protocol used afterwards is the operator's choice; several routing paradigms and protocols may coexist inside an area; the routing adjacency topology and the transport topology are not assumed to match; and the requirements must allow the architecture to evolve.
sections.eli5: Imagine a country that divides itself into regions, and each region picks its own way of drawing maps. This memo says what the regions must agree on, without telling anyone which maps to draw.

sections.title: Routing Areas and Routing Controllers
sections.content:
The basic unit is the Routing Area (RA), a partition of the network. Routing services for one RA come from a Routing Performer, which may be built from distributed Routing Controllers (RCs). The RCs get topology information from Link Resource Managers (LRMs), store it in a Routing Information Database (RDB), and cooperate so that every copy of the RDB stays in step.

The RC itself is protocol independent. Actual protocol messages are handled by Protocol Controllers (PCs), carried over the control plane's Signaling Control Network. Several different PCs may serve one RA.

RAs nest by containment: a parent RA contains child RAs, which can contain further RAs. The RFC does not say how many levels must be supported. Before two RCs communicate they MUST verify they are bound to the same parent RA. An RA ID provides the scope for communication, and each RC needs an RC ID that MUST be unique within its RA. Every RA in a carrier's network SHALL be uniquely identifiable.

One resilience rule stands out: failure of an RC, or of communication between RCs, MUST NOT disrupt calls already established. Calls still being set up may fail, and call setup may be unavailable during recovery.
sections.eli5: Think of boxes inside boxes, like a country, its states and their towns. Each town has a map keeper, and they must all know which box they belong to and have a name no other keeper in the town shares. If a map keeper gets sick, phone calls already going on must not be cut off.

sections.title: Sharing Routing Information Between Levels
sections.content:
Routing information may flow between RCs at adjacent levels, called Level N and Level N+1. Communication happens only between a parent and a child. RCs of one RA never talk to RCs of another RA at the same level. If information is exchanged, it SHOULD include reachability and MAY include node and link topology, depending on policy. The intra-RA links of a child can be hidden from its parent.

Information going up and information going down can form a feedback loop when both carry reachability. So the routing protocol MUST include a method to stop information passed from one level to another from being re-introduced to where it came from, and it SHALL tell apart information originated at a given level from information derived from other RAs.

If several RCs in one RA transform (filter or summarize) and forward information to other levels, the result at the receiving level must be self-consistent. The RFC describes two ways to connect levels: both routing functions in one system, where the interface is internal but re-advertisement MUST be consistent, or separate systems, where the interface is out of scope.

Summarizing topology can reduce the accuracy of routing and may require additional path calculation.
sections.eli5: Towns tell their state what places can be reached, and the state tells towns about the rest of the country. The rule is that a message must never bounce back to where it started, or everyone would go round in circles.

sections.title: Configuration and Evolution
sections.content:
An RC MUST support static, operator-assisted configuration of its parent and child relationships, including RA ID and RC ID. It MAY support automated configuration. The same applies to its adjacencies with other RCs in the RA. The routing protocol SHOULD support all the adjacency types of G.7715 section 9, including congruent topology with distributed RCs and hubbed topology.

Containment can change, for example because of mergers, acquisitions and divestitures. The routing protocol SHOULD support changes in the number of RA levels and the aggregation and segmentation of RAs. It is not expected to start or run those operations by itself. Reconfiguring the hierarchy may not disrupt calls in progress, though calls being set up may fail.
sections.eli5: A person sets up who belongs to which box, and the system can help but does not have to do it alone. If companies merge and the boxes get rearranged, existing phone calls should keep going.

sections.title: Routing Attributes for Nodes and Links
sections.content:
Attributes are grouped as node or link related, provisioned or negotiated or automatically configured, and inherited from a server layer or specific to a layer. Inheritance can avoid repeating configuration. ASON's control plane stand-in for a transport resource is the SubNetwork Point (SNP), and a group of them for routing purposes is an SNP Pool (SNPP). Routing sees topology as SNPP links, and the control plane view is not assumed to match the physical topology.

Advertisements MAY carry the RA ID, the RC ID of the originator, information to identify an advertisement and tell whether it was updated, and an indication that it was derived from a different level.

For nodes, Node ID is REQUIRED in both capability and usage, and Reachability is REQUIRED as a capability but OPTIONAL in usage. For links, the local and remote SNPP link IDs are REQUIRED (the remote ID is optional when the far end is outside the RA). Link characteristics are listed in a table in the RFC: Signal Type, Link Weight, Resource Class, Local Connection Types and Link Capacity are REQUIRED capabilities; Link Availability, Diversity Support and Local Adaptation Support are OPTIONAL. Capability means what a link state protocol must support, and usage means how much operator control should be available.
sections.eli5: Each place and each road gets a short fact card: its name, what it connects to, how big it is and how costly it is to use. Some cards must always be filled in, and others are optional extras.

sections.title: Security and Conclusions
sections.content:
The ASON routing protocol MUST deliver the operational security objectives where required. The ITU-T objectives of confidentiality, integrity and accountability may vary in importance and do not necessarily require anything from the routing protocol itself, since other established means can meet them. A threat analysis of a proposed protocol SHOULD address masquerade, eavesdropping, unauthorized access, loss or corruption of information including replay, repudiation, forgery and denial of service.

The conclusions repeat the main rules. RAs are uniquely identified; there is no one-to-one tie between an RA and a routing protocol; the routing adjacency topology and transport topology SHALL NOT be assumed congruent; routing must support multiple links between nodes and RAs; and the protocol SHALL converge so that the distributed RDBs become synchronized. A subnetwork or RA MUST be able to present itself to the wider network as a single logical entity with only its external links visible.
sections.eli5: The memo says the system must stay safe from snoops, fakes and floods, but that other tools can do part of that job. Its last reminder is that each box should look like a single dot to everyone outside it.

items.title: Routing Controller (RC)
items.text: Handles routing information and exchanges it with peer RCs by operating on the RDB. Protocol independent.

items.title: Link Resource Manager (LRM)
items.text: Supplies link information to the RC and reports state changes.

items.title: Protocol Controller (PC)
items.text: Handles protocol-specific message exchanges. Protocol dependent.

items.title: Routing Database (RDB)
items.text: Repository for local topology, network topology, reachability and other routing information.
